name: Obolo
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Obolo (obol1243) is not in the catalog. The sweep lists two stress-titled works, both Faraclas 1984. (1) JWAL 14(1) 'Tone and phrase stress: the extra high tone in Obolo' was already on file from the earlier pass today (open JWAL archive PDF + 300-dpi scanned) and was read in full: it is the first-hand, instrumentally backed description of Obolo suprasegmentals — three tonemes plus a PHRASE-stress system with one stress per syntactic stress group, placed by ranked phonological/morphosyntactic/pragmatic criteria, with extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes automatically stressed; no word-stress rule exists. (2) JALL 6(2) 'Tone, stress, and the Obolo verbal focus system' (doi 10.1515/jall.1984.6.2.127) is closed everywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, CrossRef; de Gruyter/Brill page WAF-blocked; not on archive.org/CORE; HathiTrust Cloudflare-blocked) — medium priority, expected to be the phrase-stress/focus application rather than a word-stress statement. Also on file and consistent: Faraclas 1982 JWAL 12(2): 77 (primary sentence stress on one syllable per rhythm group) and Connell 1994 JWAL 24(1): 12 (only Faraclas 1984 has investigated phrasal stress in Lower Cross). Not obtainable: Faraclas 1984 'A grammar of Obolo' (IULC; CORE/MPG.PuRe record only, no text), Faraclas 'A phonology of the western dialects of Obolo' (cited as forthcoming; fn. 1 says its ch. 6-7 hold the stress/tone material; no published record), Rowland-Oke 2003 (Google Books feed gives blurb only; Books JSON API over daily quota). New web records appended to under a dated addendum. Recommended catalog entry: tone language, phrase-level stress only, no word stress; deciding source Faraclas 1984 JWAL pp. 4-5, 9-11.

new_statements.quote: In Obolo, each syllable of a noun is assigned one tone lexically, while each verb stem is assigned a single tone (high or low) which is distributed suprasegmentally over however many syllables it may contain. The systems of lexical tone and downdrift, however, coexist and interact with other suprasegmental systems, including a system of phrasal stress. [p. 4] ... Intonation patterns are realized over pause groups, which are usually bounded by pauses before and after, as the name would suggest. Phrase stress is realized over stress groups, which are usually smaller than pause groups (although the two may coincide over one single phrase). One phrase stress is assigned to each stress group in a given utterance. [p. 5]
new_statements.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1984. Tone and phrase stress: The extra high tone in Obolo. Journal of West African Languages 14(1): 3-17.
new_statements.locator: pp. 4-5 (section 1, 'Phrase stress in Obolo'); further pp. 9-11 on which syllable of the stress group is stressed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (15-page A4 scan, no text layer: extracted text on pp. 1-3 yields 3 bytes, so the scanned was justified). Rendered pp. 1-3 of the scan to images and compared with ocr_faraclas1984/printed page = scanned page + 2). Title page (printed p. 3): 'Journal of West African Languages XIV, 1 (1984) 3 / TONE AND PHRASE STRESS: THE EXTRA HIGH TONE IN OBOLO / Nicholas Faraclas / University of Port Harcourt, University of California, Berkeley' (the scanned dropped the first title line; the citation is right). Both halves of the quoted passage are present verbatim: printed p. 4 para 2 'In Obolo, each syllable of a noun is assigned one tone lexically, while each verb stem is assigned a single tone (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Obolo is a tone language (three tonemes: high, low, extra high; nouns carry a tone per syllable, verb stems a single H or L). Stress exists only at the phrase level: each syntactically defined 'stress group' (a verb phrase with its arguments, an adverbial complement, or a detached noun phrase; each serial verb and indirect object is its own group) receives exactly one phrase stress, cued by extra-high pitch, higher amplitude and extra length. Which syllable within the group carries it is not fixed by word position: stress gravitates to underlyingly non-low syllables and group boundaries (phonological), to extra-high-toned verbal prefixes, the first morpheme of a place/time/manner complement, extra-high verb roots and prominent subject NPs (morphosyntactic), and follows verb-focus patterns (semantic-pragmatic). Certain extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive i, question words, interjections, imperatives) are automatically stressed. No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Faraclas 1984 p. 11: 'In some cases, the stress seems to distribute itself evenly over two or even three syllables'; Faraclas 1982 p. 77: 'Primary sentence stress is usually assigned to one syllable of this [rhythm] group. Serialized verbs and indirect object phrases... as well as complements of time, manner, or location tend to detach themselves from the rest of the sentence, receiving secondary stress in most cases.'
new_statements.exceptions: Under information-question, imperative, negative, exclamatory, hypothetical and indirect-discourse intonation only the first stress group of a pause group receives phrase stress (p. 11-12). Extra high tone on noun stems occurs 'in cases where there is no apparent reason to postulate accent or stress at any level' (p. 13), i.e. lexical extra high is not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phrase ('stress group'), not the word; data are connected speech and read sentences with F0 measurements from the University of Ibadan phonetics lab. Language is tonal, so the secondary reading 'tonal-with-stress-statement' also applies. Vowel-length table (p. 5) shows stressed vowels ~215-245 ms vs unstressed 118-181 ms. Analysis is of the Western dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Faraclas's data are explicitly from the "Western dialects of Obolo" (title of Faraclas 1982; fn. 1 of Faraclas 1984 says the material comes from his "A Phonology of the Western Dialects of Obolo", to appear). Connell 2016 (SPiL Plus 48: 11) notes Faraclas 1984 is based on one dialect and that eastern coastal varieties remain undocumented. Glottolog 5.3 lists no dialect-level languoids under obol1243, so no dialect glottocode can be given.

The systems of lexical tone and downdrift, however, coexist and interact with other suprasegmental systems, including a system of phrasal stress. [...] Phrase stress is realized over stress groups, which are usually smaller than pause groups (although the two may coincide over one single phrase). new_statements.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1984. Tone and phrase stress: The extra high tone in Obolo. Journal of West African Languages 14(1): 3-17.
new_statements.reading: Obolo is a tone language (H, L, extra high) with no word-level stress: the only stress described is phrasal, one per syntactically delimited stress group, its syllable chosen by phonological, morphosyntactic and pragmatic hierarchies (p. 9), with a set of extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes (negative, future, 3sg completive, question words) that are automatically stressed (pp. 10-11). Corroborated first-hand by Faraclas 1982 JWAL 12(2): 77 ('Primary sentence stress is usually assigned to one syllable of this [rhythm] group', already on file) and second-hand by Connell 1994 JWAL 24(1): 12 (Lower Cross tone 'complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done'). If a catalog record is created, the coding should be: tone language, stress is phrase-level (culminative per stress group, syntactically/pragmatically placed), no lexical/word stress.

sources.note: Obolo has three tonemes (H, L, extra high) plus a system of PHRASE stress: one phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group (verb phrase, adverbial complement, detached NP); cues are extra-high F0, amplitude, length; which syllable in the group is stressed follows phonological > morphosyntactic > semantic-pragmatic hierarchies; some extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive, question words) are automatically stressed; stress may spread over 2-3 syllables; no word-level stress rule is given (pp. 4-5, 9-11).

sources.note: p. 77: 'Preliminary stress and intonation studies indicate that, in Obolo statement intonation, the speech chain divides itself into rhythm groups centered either around a verb or around a complement of time, location, or manner... Primary sentence stress is usually assigned to one syllable of this group. Serialized verbs and indirect object phrases... as well as complements of time, manner, or location tend to detach themselves from the rest of the sentence, receiving secondary stress in most cases.' Phrase-level only.
